title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text:
Español
Filling raised beds and big planters takes more soil than most people expect, and bags add up fast. This works out the volume for beds, round pots and tree planters, and shows how to cut the cost of deep beds.

title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text:
Tips for filling beds

A raised bed 4 × 8 ft and 12 in deep holds about 1.2 cubic yards (32 ft³) once settled. That’s over 20 bags of 1.5 ft³.
Fill in layers and water each one so the soil settles before you plant.
Top up each spring. Beds sink as organic matter breaks down; an inch or two of compost each year keeps them full.
Avoid treated wood scraps as filler, and anything painted or glued.

title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text:
Pots and potting mix

Potting mix is sold in quarts or cubic feet in the US (8 qt, 16 qt, 1–2 cu ft) and in litres elsewhere. One cubic foot is about 26 quarts or 28 litres.
Nursery “gallon” sizes are trade sizes, not measurements. A #1 (“1-gallon”) pot holds about 3 quarts; a #5 holds about 4 gallons.
Use potting mix, not garden soil, in pots. Garden soil packs down in containers and stays waterlogged at the bottom.

title: Africa - the Beginning
text:
Mosi-oa-Tunya (Victoria Falls) meaning “the smoke that thunders”.



Where it began
RafikiArdhi grew out of years of soil research on the rooi (red) plane of Stellenbosch University, teaching and agricultural extension across Africa. From university-based work in South Africa to working alongside farmers throughout southern, central and eastern Africa, these experiences shaped a belief that scientific knowledge should support both ecosystem and human wellbeing.
The work continues through practical tools and approaches that make science more accessible, locally relevant and useful for the people who depend on the land.


The land
The complexity of Africa’s landscapes and soil is sometimes hidden beneath the surface, but a hike into the Cape Fold Belt can reveal the beauty and intricacy of the land.



Muizenberg Mountain summit (not to be confused with the town) with Stellenbosch below and False Bay and Table Mountain in the Distance.


From a mountain summit, you can begin to appreciate the geological history that shaped these landscapes. It can also boggle the mind that penguins live just a 45-minute drive from the cliffs of Muizenberg.



Penguins can be found on beaches of Cape Peninsula with the most popular being Boulders Beach.


The academic and environmental setting of Stellenbosch provides an ideal place to develop scientific skills while learning why they matter beyond the university. This setting brought awards to the people who helped build RafikiArdhi in its early research, and the chance to do research while seeing why it matters.


The people
Blessed by diversity and contrasts, Africa offers people from every background and experience to learn from. From waking early to collect water for the day to shopping at the local market, everyday life is shaped by community. Collaboration happens naturally, often without anyone thinking of it as collaboration. Bringing ideas together is part of the day, not a job.



People celebrating Siku ya Uhuru (Independence Day) on December 9th, 2011 in Boma Ng’ombe Tanzania.


We learned geostatistics in Zambia, community-based agriculture in Malawi, agricultural policy in Namibia, sustainable agricultural intensification in South Africa, the importance of smallholder farms in Tanzania, dryland water management in Kenya and the value of agricultural extension on highly leached soil in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. None of these lessons stands alone. This community thinking gave us the opportunity to base our research on increasing access to information and digital soil mapping for farms, aspects that were rarely researched at the time.
The people and cultures are diverse, but the creative freedom to learn, adapt and bring ideas together remains the same.



Agriculture festival in Lusaka, Zambia with the President making the keynote speech.




Where connections were built, and still last.
The work doesn’t end when a project does, or when we leave a place. Ideas travel, collaborations continue, and lessons from one landscape find meaning in another. The connections built through research, teaching, and shared experiences across Africa continue to shape how we approach scientific problems today. RafikiArdhi carries that spirit forward: bringing knowledge together, making tools accessible, and creating space for new ideas to grow.
We continue to work with people connected to organisations such as Phyla Earth in Lusaka, Zambia; Stellenbosch University in South Africa; Zambia Institute of Agriculture in Ndola, Zambia; and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture, with work across West and East Africa.



Group of multidisciplinary scientists from Stellenbosch University, not an academic meeting but forming connections.


These relationships are not maintained simply for commercial gain. They endure because research is a collective effort, built on cumulative knowledge and the contributions of many people. It takes a village.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
Español
Measure your area, pick a material, and see how much to order: in cubic yards, tons, bags or pallets. Odd shapes are fine: add them up piece by piece and subtract patios or paths. Every number shows how it was calculated, so you can check it against a supplier’s quote.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
How to measure

Rectangles and squares: length × width. An L-shaped bed is two rectangles; add them as two pieces.
Circles: measure straight across the middle (the diameter). For a ring around a tree, add the full circle and subtract the inner circle.
Triangles: measure all three sides. You don’t need the height.
Curvy beds: run a tape measure along the longest straight line through the bed. Every few feet, measure straight across at a right angle. Enter those widths in order, including both ends (0 if the bed comes to a point). The more widths you measure, the more accurate the area.

title: Landscape materials calculator
section: Why order more than you measured
text:
Why order more than you measured
Loose soil, compost and mulch settle once they are spread and watered, and road base or sand shrinks when it is compacted. The calculator adds a typical allowance for each material; you can change it under Assumptions. It then rounds up to the next half unit, because suppliers rarely sell less.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
Cubic yards vs tons
Soil, compost and mulch are usually sold by the cubic yard (volume). Stone, gravel and sand are usually sold by the ton (weight). The same cubic yard can weigh anywhere from about 600 lb (mulch) to over 2,500 lb (gravel), so a price per ton and a price per yard cannot be compared without knowing the weight. Ask your supplier what their material weighs per yard, and put that number in Assumptions.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
Before you buy topsoil
“Topsoil” has no legal definition, and quality varies a lot. Before you buy, ask:

Is it screened? Screened soil has had rocks, roots and clods removed.
What is in it? Native soil, a blend with compost or sand, or fill dirt?
Has it been tested? Ask for pH, organic matter, salts and texture. A reputable supplier can tell you.
Can I see it first? Look for weeds, construction debris, plastic or a sour smell. When the load arrives, check that it matches what you saw.

Don’t pay for more than you need: a quote for several times the volume this calculator gives is worth questioning.

title: Rain garden and dry well calculator
text:
Español
A rain garden is a shallow planted dip that catches runoff from a roof or driveway and lets it soak in. A dry well does the same job underground, in a pit filled with gravel. Both depend on how fast your soil drains, so do a drainage test first.

title: Rain garden and dry well calculator
text:
Building a rain garden

Location: a low spot at least 10 ft from the house, where water already heads, but not where it stands for days.
Shape: longer than it is wide, across the slope, with a level bottom so water spreads evenly.
Inlet and overflow: line the inlet with stone so it doesn’t erode, and give the overflow a safe path for storms bigger than the design.
Plants: wet-tolerant species in the bottom, drought-tolerant ones on the rim. Native plants with deep roots keep the soil open.
Soil: if your soil drains poorly, mix compost into the bottom, but don’t create a “bathtub” of loose soil in dense clay. An underdrain is the fix for very slow soils.

title: Build: problem solving
text:
Some environmental questions don’t have an off-the-shelf answer. That’s where we start.


When the data runs out
No survey, no gauges, no budget for fieldwork. We build defensible answers from what already exists, and we’re honest about what that costs in certainty.


Don’t start over
Old surveys and past projects are worth more than people think. We update and combine what has already been paid for instead of starting again.


New problem, new method
When no method fits, we design one, test it and write it down so others can check it.


How sure are we?
Every answer comes with its uncertainty. Knowing where a map can’t be trusted is as valuable as the map.


From results to decisions
Turning model outputs into choices people can act on, explained so your funder, your council and your neighbour all understand it.


Glass box, not black box
Methods you can open up and audit, tested against AI rather than replaced by it.


Beyond the free tools
The deeper version of any tool on this site, built for your problem.





New problem, new method: soil organic carbon across Malawi in one map. Colour shows how carbon is shared between 0–30, 30–60 and 60–100 cm. Shade shows whether it is increasing or decreasing over time.


You receive a licence to use the methods and results built for you. RafikiArdhi keeps the methods themselves and may later release an open version. Engineering work that requires a licensed professional engineer is carried out alongside that engineer.

title: Drip irrigation calculator
text:
Español
Drip puts water at the roots, but run times are usually guesses. Enter what each plant needs and what your emitters deliver; this works out the run time and checks that the zone can supply it.

title: Drip irrigation calculator
text:
Tips

Water deeply, less often. Infrequent, longer runs wet a deeper root zone than daily short ones, and deep roots handle heat better.
Emitters belong at the edge of the roots, not against the trunk or stem. For trees and shrubs that means moving them outward as the plant grows.
New plantings need more frequent water for their first season. Established native and low-water plants often need little or none outside drought.
Check the filter and flush the lines each spring. Clogged emitters are the most common reason a drip zone stops working.

title: Soil pH calculator: lime and sulfur
text:
Español
Changing soil pH takes more material on clay than on sand, and it happens slowly. This estimates how much ground limestone (to raise pH) or elemental sulfur (to lower it) you need, and tells you when lowering pH isn’t realistic.

title: Soil pH calculator: lime and sulfur
text:
Why pH changes slowly
Soil is buffered: clay and organic matter hold large reserves of acidity (or alkalinity) that resist change. That’s why clay needs two or three times as much lime as sand, and why the same amount works slowly.
Lowering pH in alkaline soils is a special case. Many soils in dry regions contain free lime (calcium carbonate), which fizzes in vinegar. Any acid you add, including sulfur as it breaks down, is used up dissolving that lime before the pH moves. Even 1% lime takes well over 100 lb of sulfur per 1,000 ft² just to neutralise. That’s why gardeners in those regions do better choosing plants suited to their soil.
The rates here are typical extension values for the top 6 inches. A lab “lime requirement” or “buffer pH” result is more accurate for your soil when you have one.

title: New-build yard soil check
text:
Español
On many new-build lots, the topsoil is scraped off during construction, the subsoil is compacted by heavy machinery, and a thin layer of soil is spread back on top before the sod goes down. Lawns and plants then struggle for years. A few simple checks show whether that’s what happened.
You’ll need: a shovel, a long screwdriver, and moist (not soggy) soil, a day or two after rain or watering.

title: New-build yard soil check
text:
Why this matters
Topsoil is the layer where roots, water and soil life do most of their work. Subsoil compacted by trucks and graders can be as dense as a road base: roots can’t enter it and water can’t drain through it. Sod laid on a thin layer over it looks fine for a season, then thins out, browns in summer and floods after storms.
Fixing it costs far less before planting than after, so check before you invest in landscaping.

Check a result
text:

title: Check a result
text:
Finding the right pixel size
Grid resolution is often chosen by habit (30 m because that’s Landsat). Hengl (2006) set out rules that tie it to what the data can actually support. For each aspect of a dataset they give a coarsest legible resolution (the largest pixel that still represents it), a finest legible resolution (below which pixels “are probably just waste of memory”) and a recommended compromise. Fill in whatever you know; the overall range is where the rules agree.



Reference
Hengl, T. (2006). Finding the right pixel size. Computers & Geosciences 32, 1283–1298. doi:10.1016/j.cageo.2005.11.008

title: Check a result
text:
Back-transformation
A mean calculated on log values, then exponentiated, is the median (geometric mean), not the mean. For skewed soil properties the difference is often 10–30%. Enter the value on the log scale.



References

Rebuild a reported stock from its inputs. If it doesn’t match, the check tries the common slips (% vs g/kg, stones ignored or on the wrong basis, organic matter instead of carbon, kg/m² vs Mg/ha) and tells you which one reproduces the reported number.

title: Check a result
text:
Area from a confusion matrix
Counting pixels in a map gives biased class areas, because every map has errors. With a stratified accuracy sample, the confusion matrix gives unbiased areas with confidence intervals (Olofsson et al. 2014). Rows are map classes, columns are reference classes, and the last column is each map class’s mapped area.



Reference
Olofsson, P., Foody, G.M., Herold, M., Stehman, S.V., Woodcock, C.E., Wulder, M.A. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148, 42–57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

title: Check a result
text:
Effective sample size
Samples close together carry overlapping information. For estimating an average, a cluster of ten nearby samples can be worth little more than one. This uses the variogram to work out how many independent samples your layout is really worth.

text:
Independence and study design BETA
Independence is a property of the study design and the question being asked, not a box that a single diagnostic can certify. Use this guided check to identify common sources of dependence and mismatches between the sampling unit, statistical analysis, and validation design. It flags issues to investigate; it does not automatically invalidate a study. If you know how many observations and groups there are, it also shows how much the grouping shrinks the effective sample size.

title: Check a result
text:
Statistical assumptions check BETA
A guided check for matching assumptions to the statistical method. Select the method and the diagnostics you have checked, then use the prompts to identify anything that may need further investigation. If you have the residuals, paste them: the check reports skewness, outliers, unequal spread, curvature and, for ordered data, autocorrelation, with a residual plot.



Scope note
This beta tool is a structured checklist, not a test of model assumptions. The relevant assumptions depend on the exact statistical procedure and intended inference. An unchecked item only means that you have not marked the check as reported. The residual diagnostic screens one set of residuals; it does not replace a full model diagnosis.

title: Check a result
text:
Model comparison audit BETA
Use this checklist when your work claims that one model performs better than another. It checks comparability of the evaluation design. With paired fold scores it also tests the difference properly (cross-validation folds share training data, so a plain paired t-test is too optimistic), and with the counts of cases where two classifiers disagree it runs McNemar’s test.



Scope note
This beta check examines the comparability of model evaluations based on your selected answers, and tests a difference only from the paired scores or counts you enter. For spatial, temporal or grouped data, validation design should reflect the intended prediction task; see Roberts et al. (2017), Ecography, 40, 913–929. doi:10.1111/ecog.02881.

text:
Coordinates and distances
A degree of longitude shrinks with latitude, so distances calculated directly on longitude and latitude are distorted, and “metres” computed from degrees are wrong. Convert a distance, or paste coordinates to check them.



Method
No paper needed: standard spherical geometry (haversine formula, mean Earth radius 6,371 km).

title: Services
text:
The tools on this site are free. What we charge for is the thinking behind them: working out what a question really needs, building methods where none exist, and checking that conclusions hold up.
For homeowners, we bring actual science to everyday decisions about soil, water and gardens, so you’re not guessing or relying on a sales pitch. For researchers, we bring creativity: new angles on hard problems, without giving up rigour. Either way, some questions don’t have an off-the-shelf answer, and that’s where we start.

title: Services
text:
Why be creative in science?
The problem. Maps treat soil as a stack of flat layers, so properties jump at every boundary and anything between the standard depths is lost.
The insight. Soil isn’t layered like a spreadsheet. It forms as one connected profile, so a map should reflect this information.
The result. Every pixel now holds a continuous, physically consistent profile. Properties can be read at any depth or totalled over the whole profile, and moisture or temperature can be added to the same framework.



Soil organic carbon: maps at six standard depths (left) and the whole-profile total (right). Turning a 2D GIS system into a depth aware 3D tool

title: Fertilizer label calculator
text:
Español
The three numbers on a fertilizer bag (N-P-K) are percentages by weight. A 20 lb bag of 24-0-6 contains 4.8 lb of nitrogen; the rest is the other nutrients and filler. This turns the label into how much product to spread, and shows what you’re really paying per pound of nutrient.

title: Fertilizer label calculator
text:
Reading a fertilizer label

N (nitrogen) drives green leafy growth. It’s the nutrient lawns need most, and it doesn’t stay in soil long, which is why it’s applied regularly.
P (phosphate, P₂O₅) supports roots and establishment. The label shows phosphate, not pure phosphorus: elemental P is about 44% of the P₂O₅ number.
K (potash, K₂O) helps with stress tolerance. Elemental K is about 83% of the K₂O number.
Slow-release or organic products feed over weeks rather than days. The arithmetic is the same; they’re just gentler.

More is not better. Extra nitrogen means more mowing, weaker roots and nitrate washing into waterways. A soil test tells you whether you need phosphate or potash at all.

title: Covariance Distance Explorer
Compost mix calculator (greens and browns)
text:
Español
A compost pile works fastest at a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of about 25–35 and moisture like a wrung-out sponge. Too much nitrogen (greens) and it smells; too much carbon (browns) and it barely heats up. Enter what you’re adding, by the bucket or any equal measure.

title: Compost mix calculator (greens and browns)
text:
Greens and browns

Greens (nitrogen-rich, usually wet): grass clippings, kitchen scraps, coffee grounds, fresh garden plants, manure.
Browns (carbon-rich, usually dry): dry leaves, straw, wood chips, sawdust, cardboard, newspaper.

Note that “parts” are by volume, and materials differ a lot in weight: a bucket of grass clippings weighs several times a bucket of dry leaves. That’s why roughly 2–3 buckets of browns to 1 of greens often balances.
Keep out: meat, dairy and oily food (attract pests), pet and human waste, diseased plants, weeds with seeds (unless your pile gets hot), and anything treated with herbicide. Some herbicides survive composting and damage vegetables.

section: From one landscape to the whole planet
text:
From one landscape to the whole planet
Some questions cannot be answered in one country. How much soil does the world have left in good condition? Who is responsible for it? How do we value something that takes centuries to form and a few seasons to lose?
In Australia, RafikiArdhi team members worked on exactly these questions. We served on the Secretariat of Aroura, the soil and soil security think tank in Sydney, during its launch and the first Global Soil Security Summit, where the Soil Security Declaration was signed. We co-authored two of Aroura’s publications and took part in projects that looked at soil at the scale of the planet.



Declaration signed by the Soil Security Think Tank memeber, written by the secretariate

title: Global – Soil Security as Shared Ground
text:
Soil security
Soil security asks a simple question with a complicated answer: is the soil able to keep providing what people and ecosystems need from it? Answering it means looking at more than the soil itself. It brings together the condition of the soil, what it is capable of, its value, how connected people are to it, and the policies and laws that govern how it is used.



Wetland in a Sydney Park, Sydney plagued by contamination from past industrial activity and current land development


That framing did not changed how we work. A soil map or a carbon stock is only part of the picture. The same soil can be secure in one place and at risk in another, depending on who depends on it and how it is managed. This is how we always worked.
What did change is that one place cannot decide these standards for another, and local knowledge is often the most useful tool.

title: Global – Soil Security as Shared Ground
text:
Thinking globally, working locally
Global projects can feel far removed from a farm, a catchment or a backyard. For us they did the opposite. They showed that the same ideas apply at every scale: know the soil, know the people who depend on it, and make the knowledge useful to them.
That thinking runs through the other places we have worked and through the research tools we share freely. The scale changes; the responsibility does not. We continue to support projects globally from young scientists to large scale projects:

title: Soils4Africa mapping
text:
Soil properties mapped consistently with depth across Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa, so that maps no longer jump at every layer boundary. The research formed part of Soils4Africa, an EU Horizon 2020 project building an open-data Soil Information System to help farmers, agri-businesses, scientists and policymakers by improving the quality and availability of African soil data.



Agricultural land across the study area in Namibia, South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini.


Sampling was sparse, only two horizons were sampled per profile, and the environmental gradients were extreme, so we developed a new method for the project: Integrated Soil Profile Mapping (ISPM). It builds on our earlier physics-informed depth spline (phySpline) and is now being extended to update existing soil maps and support decisions. See Cumulative knowledge.






Humid highlands: eSwatini, near Sheba Rock.







Savanna: a storm over a dry sand river in Kruger.







Desert: dunes of the Namib. Soil organic carbon, organisms and water are present under the surface.

title: Our own backyard, Colorado
text:
We test our homeowner tools where it matters most to us: at home.
The yard had a compacted, uneven surface, patchy drainage, an irregular shape that made the area easy to misjudge, and a 1 m drop along the left fence line, where the fence and part of the yard were slowly slumping into the neighbour’s property.
We turned the lawn edges and bare ground into gravel paths, raised beds and drip irrigation, working out every quantity of soil, mulch and gravel first with the same free calculators on our Homeowners page.



Before and after: bare ground and lawn edges turned into gravel beds and a raised garden bed.





The legal boss and professional hole digger checks the new raised bed. The wet circles show where each drip emitter waters the soil.

title: Cumulative knowledge
text:
Environmental knowledge keeps getting reset. A new survey, a new map or a new project arrives, and the last one is quietly replaced, along with everything it cost and everything it knew.
We’re working on the opposite: updating what is known as new data arrives, so that knowledge accumulates and uncertainty falls with each round instead of starting over. In Limpopo, South Africa, a continental soil survey is used to update regional soil fertility maps into domains that support land-use decisions.



Soil fertility domains across Limpopo Province, South Africa, ordered from lowest (1) to highest (9) fertility, from updating a regional map with a continental survey.


The method is an updated version of our ISPM digital soil mapping framework, built on the idea that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. The updating is physics-based: it obeys the laws of thermodynamics and is solved exactly with calculus, rather than learned by AI. Every update can be traced, checked and explained, and the knowledge it adds is never lost to a black box.
(Manuscript under production)

title: De-bushing and the soil system
text:
Invasive bush is spreading across Southern African rangelands, choking grazing land and water. Clearing it can restore land, livelihoods and can be used as a source of biofuel for cooking or energy; however, what does it do to the ecosystem we cannot see?



Shade is scarce in encroached bushveld, for people and wildlife alike.


As a research consultant to SLU (the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences) on SteamBioAfrica, an EU Horizon 2020 project turning invasive woody biomass into products that benefit local communities, we modelled soil carbon dynamics during and after de-bushing and pesticide use in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa.



Crop residue left on bare soil after clearing: what stays on the surface shapes whats underneath your feet.

title: World Bank carbon credits
text:
Carbon credits depend on knowing how much carbon is in the soil before anything changes. For a World Bank–funded carbon credit programme in Mpumalanga, South Africa, we created the baseline soil carbon stock maps using spatial mixed models, which account for how carbon varies across the landscape and how confident each estimate is.
These baselines are the reference that every future change in soil carbon is measured against.



Illustrative example of soil organic carbon mapped with depth and summed over the whole profile, from separate work. Maps from the World Bank programme are under NDA and not shown.

title: Caribbean pedohydrology
text:
The island has never had a soil survey, yet flood models need to know how much water the soil holds and how much runs off. What makes this project different is that uncertainty propagation guides every step: the hydropedological assumptions, the models, and the decisions built on them.



Our free hydrologic soil group tool applies the standard NRCS rules to a single soil. The project goes further, with no soil survey to start from and uncertainty carried through and informs every step.

title: Soil test translator
text:
Español
Copy the numbers from your soil test report. You don’t need all of them: leave blanks for anything your report doesn’t have. The translator explains each result and, just as usefully, tells you what you don’t need to buy.

title: Soil test translator
text:
Getting a soil test
Most state university extension services run soil tests for home gardeners at low cost, as do many private labs. Ask for a routine or garden test: it usually covers pH, organic matter, salts, phosphorus, potassium and often nitrate.

Sample right. Take 10–15 small cores from across the area, 0–6 in deep for gardens and 0–4 in for lawns, mix them in a clean bucket, and send about two cups.
Sample areas separately. A vegetable bed, a lawn and a shrub border are different soils with different needs.
Every 3–4 years is enough for most gardens, unless you’re fixing a problem.

A soil test is the cheapest way to avoid buying fertilizer, compost or lime you don’t need.

    How the estimate is made
    Pixels inside the soil circle are decoded to linear RGB. Clipped highlights and very dark pixels (voids, deep shadow) are dropped, and the brightest and darkest 10% are trimmed. With a black and white card each channel is mapped with a two-point line through the card patches, which removes both the colour cast and any flare offset. title: Calculadora de barriles de lluvia y captación de agua
text:
English
Un techo junta muchísima agua: una pulgada de lluvia sobre 1,000 ft² de techo son unos 600 galones. Esta herramienta calcula cuánto junta su techo y cómo se compara con un barril de lluvia.

title: Calculadora de barriles de lluvia y captación de agua
text:
Cómo aprovecharla al máximo

Los barriles se llenan rápido y se vacían despacio. Use el agua entre una tormenta y otra para que haya espacio para la siguiente.
Una manguera porosa o una línea de goteo funcionan con la presión del barril si el barril está elevado sobre bloques; los aspersores no.
Para volúmenes más grandes, dirigir las bajantes hacia áreas con plantas o hacia un jardín de lluvia guarda el agua en el mismo suelo, muchas veces más de la que cabe en los barriles, y está permitido casi en todas partes.

title: Revisar una cotización de jardinería
text:
English
Escriba el área, la profundidad que quiere y hasta tres cotizaciones. La herramienta muestra qué profundidad cubriría de verdad cada cotización, si es más (o menos) de lo que necesita, y el precio por unidad, para que pueda comparar con justicia cotizaciones en yardas, toneladas y bolsas.

title: Revisar una cotización de jardinería
text:
Convertidor de yardas y toneladas
La tierra y el mantillo normalmente se venden por yarda cúbica; la piedra, la grava y la arena por tonelada. Esta herramienta convierte entre las dos, y muestra cuánto cubre una cantidad.

title: Revisar una cotización de jardinería
section: Por qué es difícil comparar cotizaciones
text:
Por qué es difícil comparar cotizaciones

Yardas o toneladas. Una yarda cúbica de mantillo pesa unos cientos de libras; una yarda cúbica de grava pesa bastante más de una tonelada. No se puede comparar un precio por tonelada con un precio por yarda sin saber cuánto pesa el material. La herramienta convierte con pesos típicos; pídale al proveedor los suyos.
La entrega. Un cargo de entrega repartido en una carga pequeña hace que el precio por unidad parezca alto. Compare cotizaciones por la misma cantidad.
Extra por asentamiento. El material suelto se asienta después de esparcirlo, así que una cotización justa incluye un poco más que el volumen medido, normalmente 5–25% según el material. Una cotización por el doble de lo que necesita no es “un poco extra”.
Las bolsas. El tamaño de las bolsas varía (1, 1.5, 2 o 3 pies cúbicos). Revise el tamaño antes de comparar precios por bolsa.

Use la calculadora de materiales para calcular exactamente cuánto necesita en un área de forma irregular.

title: Revisión de la pendiente alrededor de los cimientos
text:
English
El agua que se junta contra los cimientos es uno de los problemas más caros que puede tener una casa. La guía común de los códigos de construcción es que el terreno baje por lo menos 6 pulgadas en los primeros 10 pies desde la casa (como 5%). Lo puede revisar en una tarde.
Cómo medir: clave una estaca pegada a los cimientos y otra a 10 pies (3 m) hacia afuera. Amarre un hilo entre las dos y nivélelo con un nivel de hilo. En cada estaca, mida desde el hilo hasta el suelo. La caída es la medida de afuera menos la de adentro. Repita cada 10–15 pies a lo largo de cada pared.

title: Revisión de la pendiente alrededor de los cimientos
section: Otras señales de un problema de pendiente
text:
Otras señales de un problema de pendiente

Agua estancada junto a los cimientos después de llover o regar.
Mantillo o tierra amontonada contra el revestimiento, muchas veces acumulada con los años.
Bajantes que descargan justo junto a la pared.
Patios, banquetas o pozos de ventana que se hundieron y ahora se inclinan hacia la casa.
Manchas de humedad, eflorescencia (costra blanca) u olor a humedad en un sótano o espacio de acceso bajo la casa.

La mayoría de estos problemas son baratos de arreglar comparados con una reparación de cimientos.

title: Calculadora del pH del suelo: cal y azufre
text:
English
Cambiar el pH del suelo requiere más material en arcilla que en arena, y sucede despacio. Esta herramienta estima cuánta piedra caliza molida (para subir el pH) o azufre elemental (para bajarlo) necesita, y le dice cuándo bajar el pH no es realista.

title: Calculadora del pH del suelo: cal y azufre
section: Por qué el pH cambia despacio
text:
Por qué el pH cambia despacio
El suelo tiene amortiguación: la arcilla y la materia orgánica guardan grandes reservas de acidez (o alcalinidad) que resisten el cambio. Por eso la arcilla necesita dos o tres veces más cal que la arena, y por eso la misma cantidad actúa despacio.
Bajar el pH en suelos alcalinos es un caso especial. Muchos suelos de regiones secas contienen cal libre (carbonato de calcio), que burbujea con vinagre. Cualquier ácido que agregue, incluido el azufre conforme se descompone, se gasta disolviendo esa cal antes de que el pH se mueva. Aun con 1% de cal se necesitan bastante más de 100 lb de azufre por cada 1,000 ft² solo para neutralizarla. Por eso a los jardineros de esas regiones les va mejor escogiendo plantas adaptadas a su suelo.
Las dosis que se usan aquí son valores típicos de extensión agrícola para las primeras 6 pulgadas. Un resultado de laboratorio de “requerimiento de cal” o “pH buffer” es más exacto para su suelo cuando lo tiene.

title: Césped o jardín de bajo consumo: calculadora de agua
text:
English
¿Cuánta agua usa de verdad un césped comparado con las alternativas? Esta herramienta estima el riego de una temporada para la misma área sembrada de distintas maneras, según su clima y el precio del agua.

title: Césped o jardín de bajo consumo: calculadora de agua
text:
Cómo se calcula
Las plantas pierden agua por las hojas a un ritmo que depende sobre todo del clima: sol, calor, viento y aire seco. Las redes meteorológicas lo expresan como evapotranspiración de referencia (ETo): lo que usaría un pasto bien regado. Cada tipo de planta usa una parte de eso: el pasto azul de Kentucky cerca del 80%, el pasto búfalo menos de la mitad, y los arbustos de bajo consumo ya establecidos una tercera parte o menos. Se resta la lluvia que pueden aprovechar las plantas, se toma en cuenta que el riego nunca es perfectamente eficiente, y eso da el riego.
Los factores que se usan aquí son valores típicos para planear. Sirven para comparar opciones, no para programar un controlador: para eso, use la prueba de vasos.

title: Calculadora de la zona de protección de árboles
text:
English
La mayoría de las raíces de un árbol están en las primeras 12–18 pulgadas del suelo y se extienden mucho más allá de las ramas. Manejar encima, amontonar material, abrir zanjas o cambiar el nivel del terreno sobre ellas puede matar un árbol adulto, muchas veces unos años después. Antes de cualquier trabajo, cerque una zona de protección.
Mida el tronco a 4½ pies (1.4 m) del suelo. Rodéelo con una cinta para medir la circunferencia, o mida el diámetro directamente.

title: Calculadora de la zona de protección de árboles
section: Por qué los árboles se mueren después de una construcción
text:
Por qué los árboles se mueren después de una construcción
Las raíces necesitan aire tanto como agua. La compactación de los vehículos aplasta los poros del suelo; la tierra de relleno entierra las raíces demasiado hondo; las zanjas las cortan. El árbol puede verse bien una o dos temporadas, usando la energía que tiene guardada, y luego empieza a secarse de arriba hacia abajo. Para cuando ve las ramas secas, el daño se hizo años antes.
La zona que se calcula aquí aumenta con el tronco, la edad del árbol y qué tan bien aguanta la especie, siguiendo un método muy usado por los arbolistas. La regla sencilla, un pie de radio por cada pulgada de diámetro del tronco, aparece en el cálculo como comparación.

title: Programador de riego por ciclos y remojo
text:
English
Si el agua corre por la banqueta mientras los aspersores están prendidos, las cabezas están aplicando agua más rápido de lo que el suelo puede absorber. La solución no cuesta nada: riegue el mismo tiempo total en ciclos más cortos, con un remojo entre uno y otro. Esta herramienta calcula qué tan cortos y cuántos.

title: Programador de riego por ciclos y remojo
text:
Por qué funciona
El agua entra al suelo a una velocidad limitada. Un suelo arenoso puede absorber una pulgada o más por hora; la arcilla tal vez una décima de pulgada. Las cabezas de rocío muchas veces aplican más de una pulgada por hora, así que en arcilla la mayor parte de un ciclo largo escurre. En pendientes escurre todavía antes.
Los ciclos cortos paran cada vuelta antes de que el agua empiece a escurrir; el remojo deja que baje al suelo antes de la siguiente vuelta. El agua total es la misma; solo deja de perderla en la cuneta.
Las tasas de infiltración que se usan aquí son valores típicos de diseño para cada suelo y pendiente. Un suelo compactado o una capa dura cerca de la superficie (muy común en lotes de casas nuevas) las reduce mucho. Si todavía ve que escurre, acorte más los ciclos.

title: Traductor del análisis de suelo
text:
English
Copie los números de su reporte del análisis de suelo. No los necesita todos: deje en blanco lo que su reporte no tenga. El traductor explica cada resultado y, algo igual de útil, le dice lo que no necesita comprar.

title: Traductor del análisis de suelo
section: Cómo hacer un análisis de suelo
text:
Cómo hacer un análisis de suelo
La mayoría de los servicios de extensión de las universidades estatales hacen análisis de suelo para jardineros caseros a bajo costo, igual que muchos laboratorios privados. Pida un análisis de rutina o para jardín: normalmente incluye pH, materia orgánica, sales, fósforo, potasio y muchas veces nitrato.

Tome bien la muestra. Saque de 10 a 15 pequeñas muestras de toda el área, de 0 a 6 pulgadas de profundidad en jardines y de 0 a 4 pulgadas en el césped, mézclelas en una cubeta limpia y mande unas dos tazas.
Muestree cada área por separado. Una cama de hortalizas, un césped y una orilla de arbustos son suelos distintos con necesidades distintas.
Cada 3 o 4 años es suficiente para la mayoría de los jardines, a menos que esté corrigiendo un problema.

Un análisis de suelo es la forma más barata de no comprar fertilizante, composta o cal que no necesita.

title: Pruebas de suelo caseras: textura, drenaje y la prueba de la cinta
text:
English
Tres pruebas sencillas le dicen casi todo lo importante de su suelo: de qué está hecho (la textura) y qué tan rápido pasa el agua (el drenaje). La textura decide cada cuánto regar, qué tan rápido entra el agua y cómo se comporta el suelo al excavar.

title: Pruebas de suelo caseras: textura, drenaje y la prueba de la cinta
text:
Prueba del frasco (textura)

Llene un frasco de lados rectos más o menos a un tercio con tierra de la profundidad de las raíces (quite piedras, raíces y basura).
Agregue agua hasta llenar unas dos terceras partes del frasco, más una cucharadita de detergente para lavavajillas o de suavizante de agua sin sal para separar las partículas.
Agite fuerte durante 3–5 minutos, déjelo quieto y ponga un cronómetro.
Al minuto, marque la altura de la capa asentada: esa es la arena.
A las 2 horas, vuelva a marcar la altura: arena más limo.
A los 2 días (cuando el agua se aclare), marque la altura final: todo, incluida la arcilla.

title: Pruebas de suelo caseras: textura, drenaje y la prueba de la cinta
section: Prueba de la cinta (textura al tacto)
text:
Prueba de la cinta (textura al tacto)
Tome un puño de tierra del tamaño de una nuez, mójelo hasta que quede como masilla y trabájelo en la mano. Luego apriételo entre el pulgar y el índice, empujándolo hacia arriba para formar una cinta hasta que se rompa por su propio peso.

title: Pruebas de suelo caseras: textura, drenaje y la prueba de la cinta
text:
Prueba de drenaje (percolación)

Excave un hoyo de unas 12 pulgadas (30 cm) de profundidad y 6–12 pulgadas de ancho.
Llénelo de agua y deje que drene por completo. Esto moja el suelo alrededor; si se lo salta, el resultado saldrá demasiado rápido.
Llénelo otra vez. Mida la profundidad del agua, espere un tiempo fijo (una hora es fácil) y vuelva a medir.



Si el hoyo todavía tiene agua al día siguiente, haga la prueba de nuevo en otro lugar y excave más hondo para buscar una capa densa o cementada. Los problemas de drenaje casi siempre se deben a una capa de abajo, no a la tierra donde siembra.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Español
Three simple tests tell you most of what matters about your soil: what it’s made of (texture) and how fast water moves through it (drainage). Texture decides how often to water, how fast water soaks in, and how the soil behaves when you dig.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Jar test (texture)

Fill a straight-sided jar about one-third with soil from root depth (pick out stones, roots and debris).
Add water until the jar is about two-thirds full, plus a teaspoon of dishwasher detergent or salt-free water softener to separate the particles.
Shake hard for 3–5 minutes, then set it down and start a timer.
After 1 minute, mark the height of the settled layer: that’s the sand.
After 2 hours, mark the height again: sand plus silt.
After 2 days (when the water clears), mark the final height: everything, including clay.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Ribbon test (texture by feel)
Take a walnut-sized lump of soil, wet it until it’s like putty, and work it in your hand. Then press it between your thumb and finger, pushing it up into a ribbon until it breaks under its own weight.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Drainage (percolation) test

Dig a hole about 12 in (30 cm) deep and 6–12 in wide.
Fill it with water and let it drain completely. This wets the surrounding soil; skip it and the result will be too fast.
Fill it again. Measure the water depth, wait a set time (an hour is easy), and measure again.



If the hole still holds water the next day, test again somewhere else and dig deeper to look for a dense or cemented layer. Drainage problems are usually about a layer below, not the soil you plant in.

title: Calculadora de profundidad de congelamiento
text:
English
En lugares fríos el suelo se puede congelar varios pies hacia abajo. Las tuberías de agua, los cimientos y los postes de cerca que quedan arriba de esa profundidad se pueden reventar, agrietar o ser empujados hacia arriba por las heladas. Esta herramienta estima qué tan hondo llega el congelamiento en un invierno promedio y en uno frío, según su clima, la superficie y su suelo.
Necesita dos números: la temperatura promedio de su mes más frío y la de su mes más caluroso. Están en la tabla del clima de su ciudad (en Wikipedia o en su servicio meteorológico). En la montaña, use una estación a una altura parecida: la temperatura baja unos 3.5 °F por cada 1,000 pies (6.5 °C por cada 1,000 m) conforme sube.

title: Calculadora de profundidad de congelamiento
section: Por qué la profundidad de congelamiento varía tanto
text:
Por qué la profundidad de congelamiento varía tanto

El frío, y cuánto dura. Lo que importa es el índice de congelamiento: qué tan abajo de cero está, sumado cada día del invierno. Un frío largo y constante congela más hondo que uno corto e intenso.
La nieve. Un pie de nieve esponjada aísla más o menos como un par de pulgadas de placa de espuma. Las entradas de autos y los caminos a los que se les quita la nieve pierden esa cobija y se congelan más hondo.
El suelo y la humedad. El agua suelta mucho calor al congelarse, y eso frena el congelamiento. La grava seca y el relleno pedregoso se congelan mucho más hondo que la arcilla húmeda.
El suelo tibio de abajo. Donde los veranos son calurosos, el suelo guarda calor que empuja contra el congelamiento desde abajo.

title: Calculadora de profundidad de congelamiento
text:
Sobre esta estimación
Usa la misma física de flujo de calor que los métodos de ingeniería para la profundidad de congelamiento, con propiedades típicas para cada tipo de suelo. Es una estimación para un invierno promedio y uno más frío que el promedio, no un valor de diseño. Las propiedades del suelo por sí solas pueden cambiar la respuesta como en una cuarta parte. Los códigos de construcción fijan las profundidades de congelamiento con los inviernos más fríos de décadas, así que siga su código local para los cimientos.
Para más control (índice de congelamiento, densidad, contenido de agua y factores de superficie), use la herramienta de profundidad de congelamiento para investigadores (en inglés).

title: Prueba de vasos para aspersores
text:
English
La mayoría de la gente adivina los tiempos de riego de sus aspersores. La prueba de vasos mide lo que cada zona aplica de verdad, en unos 20 minutos, con unos cuantos vasos y una regla.
Cómo hacerla: coloque de 8 a 12 recipientes iguales de lados rectos (latas de atún o vasos de plástico) en cuadrícula por toda una zona, lejos de las cabezas de los aspersores. Riegue la zona de 10 a 20 minutos. Mida con una regla la profundidad del agua en cada recipiente y escríbala abajo.

title: Prueba de vasos para aspersores
text:
Qué significan los números

La tasa de aplicación es qué tan rápido la zona aplica el agua. Las cabezas de rocío (spray) suelen ser rápidas (1–2 pulgadas por hora); los rotores y las boquillas rotativas son lentos (0.3–0.7 pulgadas por hora). Las zonas con tipos de cabezas distintos necesitan tiempos distintos.
La uniformidad (DU) compara el cuarto más seco de los vasos con el promedio. Con 70% o más, la cobertura es buena. Por debajo de más o menos 55%, algunos puntos reciben menos de la mitad que otros, y agregar minutos solo encharca los puntos mojados para salvar los secos.
El multiplicador de programación. Como la cobertura nunca es perfecta, el tiempo de riego se alarga un poco para que las áreas más secas reciban suficiente. Mejor cobertura significa un multiplicador más pequeño y menos agua.

Repita la prueba en cada zona: casi nunca son iguales. Cuando conozca la tasa de una zona, el programador de ciclos y remojo revisa si su suelo puede absorberla así de rápido.

title: Calculadora de mezcla para composta (verdes y cafés)
text:
English
Una composta trabaja más rápido con una relación carbono-nitrógeno (C:N) de unos 25–35 y una humedad como la de una esponja exprimida. Con demasiado nitrógeno (verdes) huele mal; con demasiado carbono (cafés) casi no se calienta. Escriba lo que está agregando, por cubetas o cualquier medida igual.

title: Calculadora de mezcla para composta (verdes y cafés)
text:
Verdes y cafés

Verdes (ricos en nitrógeno, normalmente mojados): pasto cortado, restos de cocina, café molido usado, plantas frescas del jardín, estiércol.
Cafés (ricos en carbono, normalmente secos): hojas secas, paja, astillas de madera, aserrín, cartón, periódico.

Tome en cuenta que las “partes” son por volumen, y que los materiales pesan muy distinto: una cubeta de pasto cortado pesa varias veces lo que una cubeta de hojas secas. Por eso más o menos 2–3 cubetas de cafés por 1 de verdes muchas veces queda equilibrado.
No ponga: carne, lácteos ni comida grasosa (atraen plagas), excremento de mascotas o humano, plantas enfermas, hierbas con semillas (a menos que su composta se caliente bien) ni nada tratado con herbicida. Algunos herbicidas sobreviven al compostaje y dañan las hortalizas.

title: Calculadora de la etiqueta del fertilizante
text:
English
Los tres números de una bolsa de fertilizante (N-P-K) son porcentajes por peso. Una bolsa de 20 lb de 24-0-6 contiene 4.8 lb de nitrógeno; el resto son los otros nutrientes y relleno. Esta herramienta convierte la etiqueta en cuánto producto aplicar, y muestra lo que de verdad paga por cada libra de nutriente.

title: Calculadora de la etiqueta del fertilizante
section: Cómo leer la etiqueta de un fertilizante
text:
Cómo leer la etiqueta de un fertilizante

N (nitrógeno) impulsa el crecimiento verde de las hojas. Es el nutriente que más necesita el césped, y no se queda mucho tiempo en el suelo; por eso se aplica con regularidad.
P (fosfato, P₂O₅) ayuda a las raíces y al establecimiento de las plantas. La etiqueta muestra el fosfato, no el fósforo puro: el P elemental es como el 44% del número de P₂O₅.
K (potasa, K₂O) ayuda a resistir el estrés. El K elemental es como el 83% del número de K₂O.
Los productos de liberación lenta u orgánicos alimentan durante semanas en vez de días. La cuenta es la misma; solo son más suaves.

Más no es mejor. El nitrógeno de más significa cortar el pasto más seguido, raíces más débiles y nitrato que se va a los ríos y arroyos. Un análisis de suelo le dice si de verdad necesita fosfato o potasa.

title: ¿Debo mejorar mi suelo?
text:
English
La composta y la tierra son útiles, pero se gasta mucho dinero en enmiendas que no ayudan, o que empeoran las cosas. Conteste unas preguntas y esta herramienta le dice qué vale la pena hacer según lo que va a sembrar.

title: ¿Debo mejorar mi suelo?
text:
En resumen

Árboles: nunca mejore el hoyo de plantación. Hoyo ancho, tierra del lugar, mantillo.
Plantas nativas y de bajo consumo: normalmente nada. El suelo rico les perjudica.
Hortalizas: sí, composta cada año.
Césped: mejore el suelo antes de sembrar. En un césped que ya existe, airee y cubra con una capa ligera.
Arcilla: la composta ayuda; un poco de arena la empeora.
Agua estancada: es un problema de drenaje, no de calidad del suelo.

title: Revisión del suelo en casas nuevas
text:
English
En muchos lotes de casas nuevas, la tierra vegetal se raspa durante la construcción, el subsuelo queda compactado por la maquinaria pesada, y se esparce una capa delgada de tierra encima antes de poner el pasto en rollo. Después el césped y las plantas batallan durante años. Unas cuantas revisiones sencillas muestran si eso fue lo que pasó.
Necesita: una pala, un desarmador largo, y el suelo húmedo (no encharcado), uno o dos días después de una lluvia o un riego.

title: Revisión del suelo en casas nuevas
text:
Por qué importa
La tierra vegetal es la capa donde las raíces, el agua y la vida del suelo hacen la mayor parte de su trabajo. El subsuelo compactado por camiones y niveladoras puede quedar tan denso como la base de un camino: las raíces no pueden entrar y el agua no puede drenar. El pasto en rollo puesto sobre una capa delgada encima se ve bien una temporada, y luego se adelgaza, se pone café en verano y se inunda después de las tormentas.
Arreglarlo cuesta mucho menos antes de plantar que después, así que revíselo antes de invertir en jardinería.

title: Calculadora de riego por goteo
text:
English
El goteo lleva el agua a las raíces, pero los tiempos de riego casi siempre se adivinan. Escriba lo que necesita cada planta y lo que dan sus goteros; esta herramienta calcula el tiempo de riego y revisa que la zona pueda abastecerlo.

title: Calculadora de riego por goteo
text:
Consejos

Riegue a fondo y con menos frecuencia. Los riegos más largos y espaciados mojan una zona de raíces más profunda que los riegos cortos diarios, y las raíces profundas aguantan mejor el calor.
Los goteros van en la orilla de las raíces, no pegados al tronco o al tallo. En árboles y arbustos, eso significa moverlos hacia afuera conforme crece la planta.
Las plantas recién sembradas necesitan agua más seguido durante su primera temporada. Las plantas nativas y de bajo consumo ya establecidas muchas veces necesitan poca o nada fuera de una sequía.
Revise el filtro y purgue las líneas cada primavera. Los goteros tapados son la razón más común por la que una zona de goteo deja de funcionar.

title: Calculadora de jardín de lluvia y pozo seco
text:
English
Un jardín de lluvia es una hondonada poco profunda con plantas que recibe el agua que escurre de un techo o de una entrada de autos y deja que se absorba. Un pozo seco hace lo mismo bajo tierra, en un hoyo lleno de grava. Los dos dependen de qué tan rápido drena su suelo, así que primero haga una prueba de drenaje.

title: Calculadora de jardín de lluvia y pozo seco
section: Cómo hacer un jardín de lluvia
text:
Cómo hacer un jardín de lluvia

Ubicación: un lugar bajo, por lo menos a 10 pies de la casa, hacia donde ya va el agua, pero no donde se queda estancada por días.
Forma: más largo que ancho, atravesado a la pendiente, con el fondo a nivel para que el agua se reparta parejo.
Entrada y desborde: cubra la entrada con piedra para que no se erosione, y dele al desborde un camino seguro para tormentas más grandes que las del diseño.
Plantas: especies que toleren lo mojado en el fondo, y especies que aguanten la sequía en la orilla. Las plantas nativas de raíces profundas mantienen el suelo abierto.
Suelo: si su suelo drena mal, mezcle composta en el fondo, pero no haga una “tina” de tierra suelta dentro de arcilla densa. Para suelos muy lentos, la solución es un dren por debajo.

title: Calculadora de materiales para jardinería
text:
English
Mida su área, escoja un material y vea cuánto pedir: en yardas cúbicas, toneladas, bolsas o tarimas. Las formas irregulares no son problema: súmelas pieza por pieza y reste patios o caminos. Cada número muestra cómo se calculó, para que lo pueda comparar con la cotización de un proveedor.

title: Calculadora de materiales para jardinería
text:
Cómo medir

Rectángulos y cuadrados: largo × ancho. Una cama en forma de L son dos rectángulos; súmelos como dos piezas.
Círculos: mida de lado a lado por el centro (el diámetro). Para un anillo alrededor de un árbol, sume el círculo completo y reste el círculo de adentro.
Triángulos: mida los tres lados. No necesita la altura.
Camas con curvas: tienda una cinta métrica por la línea recta más larga que cruce la cama. Cada pocos pies, mida de lado a lado en ángulo recto. Escriba esos anchos en orden, incluidos los dos extremos (0 si la cama termina en punta). Entre más anchos mida, más exacta será el área.

title: Calculadora de materiales para jardinería
section: Por qué pedir más de lo que midió
text:
Por qué pedir más de lo que midió
La tierra suelta, la composta y el mantillo se asientan después de esparcirlos y regarlos, y la base para caminos o la arena se encogen al compactarse. La calculadora agrega un margen típico para cada material; lo puede cambiar en Supuestos. Luego redondea hacia arriba a la siguiente media unidad, porque los proveedores casi nunca venden menos.

title: Calculadora de materiales para jardinería
text:
Yardas cúbicas o toneladas
La tierra, la composta y el mantillo normalmente se venden por yarda cúbica (volumen). La piedra, la grava y la arena normalmente se venden por tonelada (peso). La misma yarda cúbica puede pesar desde unas 600 lb (mantillo) hasta más de 2,500 lb (grava), así que no se puede comparar un precio por tonelada con un precio por yarda sin saber el peso. Pregúntele a su proveedor cuánto pesa su material por yarda, y ponga ese número en Supuestos.

title: Calculadora de materiales para jardinería
text:
Antes de comprar tierra vegetal
La “tierra vegetal” (topsoil) no tiene una definición legal, y la calidad varía mucho. Antes de comprar, pregunte:

¿Está cernida? A la tierra cernida se le quitaron piedras, raíces y terrones.
¿Qué contiene? ¿Tierra natural, una mezcla con composta o arena, o tierra de relleno?
¿La han analizado? Pida el pH, la materia orgánica, las sales y la textura. Un proveedor serio se lo puede decir.
¿La puedo ver antes? Fíjese si tiene maleza, escombro de construcción, plástico u olor agrio. Cuando llegue la carga, revise que sea igual a la que vio.

No pague por más de lo que necesita: vale la pena preguntar por una cotización que pida varias veces el volumen que da esta calculadora.

title: Calculadora de tierra para camas elevadas y macetas
text:
English
Llenar camas elevadas y jardineras grandes lleva más tierra de lo que la mayoría espera, y las bolsas suman rápido. Esta herramienta calcula el volumen para camas, macetas redondas y jardineras para árboles, y muestra cómo bajar el costo de las camas profundas.

title: Calculadora de tierra para camas elevadas y macetas
text:
Consejos para llenar camas

Una cama elevada de 4 × 8 pies y 12 pulgadas de profundidad contiene unas 1.2 yardas cúbicas (32 ft³) ya asentada. Son más de 20 bolsas de 1.5 ft³.
Llene por capas y riegue cada una para que la tierra se asiente antes de sembrar.
Agregue tierra cada primavera. Las camas bajan conforme la materia orgánica se descompone; una o dos pulgadas de composta cada año las mantiene llenas.
No use restos de madera tratada como relleno, ni nada pintado o con pegamento.

title: Calculadora de tierra para camas elevadas y macetas
text:
Macetas y tierra para macetas

En EE. UU. la tierra para macetas se vende en cuartos de galón o pies cúbicos (8 qt, 16 qt, 1–2 pies³) y en litros en otros países. Un pie cúbico son unos 26 cuartos de galón o 28 litros.
Los tamaños “de galón” de vivero son medidas comerciales, no medidas reales. Una maceta #1 (“de 1 galón”) contiene unos 3 cuartos de galón; una #5 unos 4 galones.
Use tierra para macetas, no tierra del jardín, en las macetas. La tierra del jardín se compacta en los recipientes y se queda encharcada en el fondo.

title: Frost depth calculator
text:
In cold places the ground can freeze several feet down. Water lines, footings and fence posts set above that depth can burst, crack or get pushed up by frost heave. This estimates how deep frost goes in an average winter and a cold one, for your climate, surface and soil.
You need two numbers: the average temperature of your coldest month and of your warmest month. They are in the climate table for your town (on Wikipedia or your weather service). In the mountains, use a station at a similar elevation: temperatures drop about 3.5 °F per 1,000 ft (6.5 °C per 1,000 m) as you go up.

title: Frost depth calculator
section: Why frost depth varies so much
text:
Why frost depth varies so much

Cold, and how long it lasts. What matters is the freezing index: how far below freezing it is, added up over every day of winter. A long, steady cold freezes deeper than a short, sharp one.
Snow. A foot of fluffy snow insulates about as well as a couple of inches of foam board. Plowed driveways and shoveled paths lose that blanket and freeze deepest.
Soil and moisture. Water gives off a lot of heat as it freezes, which slows the frost. Dry gravel and rocky fill freeze much deeper than wet clay.
Warm ground below. Where summers are warm, the ground stores heat that pushes back against the frost from below.

title: Frost depth calculator
text:
About this estimate
This uses the same heat-flow physics as engineering frost-depth methods, with typical soil properties for each soil type. It is an estimate for an average and a colder-than-average winter, not a design value. Soil properties alone can shift the answer by about a quarter. Building codes set frost depths from the coldest winters in decades, so follow your local code for footings.
For more control (freezing index, density, water content and surface factors), use the frost depth tool for researchers.

title: Sprinkler catch-cup test
text:
Español
Most people guess their sprinkler run times. A catch-cup test measures what each zone actually puts down, in about 20 minutes, with a few cups and a ruler.
How to do it: set out 8–12 identical straight-sided containers (tuna cans or plastic cups) in a grid across one zone, away from the heads themselves. Run the zone for 10–20 minutes. Measure the water depth in each container with a ruler and enter them below.

title: Sprinkler catch-cup test
text:
What the numbers mean

Application rate is how fast the zone puts water down. Spray heads are usually fast (1–2 in/hr); rotors and rotary nozzles are slow (0.3–0.7 in/hr). Zones with different head types need different run times.
Evenness (DU) compares the driest quarter of the cups with the average. At 70% or above, coverage is good. Below about 55%, some spots get less than half as much as others, and adding minutes just floods the wet spots to rescue the dry ones.
Scheduling multiplier. Because coverage is never perfect, the run time is stretched a little so the drier areas still get enough. Better coverage means a smaller multiplier and less water.

Repeat the test for each zone: zones rarely match. Once you know a zone’s rate, the cycle-and-soak scheduler checks whether your soil can absorb it that fast.

title: Soil resilience
text:
Soil is not a random mixture. Soil organises itself over time, using and releasing energy as water, heat and carbon move through, and that organisation is what lets soil absorb shocks and performs many ecosystem services at once. We measure it with thermodynamics rather than by counting soil types: in other words, pedodiversity reflects how a soil dissipates energy relative to what it has available.



Grassland in recovery along an agroforestry system in Germany, with young trees in guards along the slope.


In the U.S. Southwest, this approach revealed agroecosystem patterns on ancestral and contemporary Indigenous lands, from the Chuska Mountains to the Great Sage Plain and Hopi Land, where generations of land use and soil organisation are written into the landscape. The original preprint focused on this area because of our knowledge of, and closeness to, the land, but it raised more questions than it answered. Humanity’s tie to the land is not unique to this region, and the questions that run from pedodiversity to pedocomplexity can be studied at many scales and with many techniques, for the wellbeing of both ecosystems and people.



From soil states with depth (A), to thermodynamic pedodiversity in three dimensions (B), to pedocomplexity (C): cultural insight and a physics-informed model, working together.


Preprint: Thermodynamic pedodiversity patterns reveal agroecosystem patterns in Indigenous lands of the U.S. Southwest

title: Soils in motion
text:
A dry sand river as a storm builds. Within hours the same channel can carry water.


Most soil science treats soil as something that sits still. We are treating it as a system in motion: water moving through it in drought and in flood, heat and energy flowing with it, and the soil organising itself around that flow over time.
The key is exergy: the share of energy a soil can actually put to work, rather than the total energy passing through it. What matters is not how much energy a soil receives, but how well it uses what it has.
That changes how soil is perceived. A desert soil can seem “dead”: bare, crusted and pale. Yet with very little rain and energy, it may be doing its jobs remarkably well. Its surface crust holds the ground together and fixes nutrients, it stores water deep where it does not evaporate, and it locks away carbon for thousands of years. A tropical soil under lush forest can look full of life, yet much of that richness sits in the plants, not the soil. Many tropical soil is deeply weathered and hold few nutrients of its own, and clear the forest and that apparent fertility can disappear within a few seasons. Judged against the energy each has available, the desert soil may function just as well for ecosystem services.
To capture this, we are bringing mathematics from outside soil science into it, linking how energy moves with how soil organises, functions and recovers. The work spans drylands to the tropics, from the Western United States to the Malawi, with a students leading the charge.



Sossusvlei, Namibia, in September. The pan stays dry for long stretches, but it can fill with water from the ephemeral Tsauchab River, and a desert bloom follows from the seed bank that survives the dry heat.


Details stay under wraps until the work is published.

RafikiArdhi begain in gardening and landscaping, developing an early connection to the land that would grow into environmental research published in international journals. title: Cycle-and-soak sprinkler scheduler
text:
Español
If water runs down the sidewalk while the sprinklers are on, your heads are putting water down faster than the soil can take it in. The fix costs nothing: run the same total time in shorter cycles, with a soak in between. This works out how short, and how many.

title: Cycle-and-soak sprinkler scheduler
text:
Why this works
Water soaks into soil at a limited rate. Sandy soil can take in an inch or more an hour; clay may take in a tenth of an inch. Spray heads often put down over an inch an hour, so on clay most of a long cycle runs off. On slopes it runs off even sooner.
Short cycles stop each round before water starts to run off; the soak lets it move down into the soil before the next round. The total water is the same; you just stop losing it to the gutter.
The intake rates used here are typical design values for each soil and slope. Compacted soil or a hard layer near the surface (very common on new-build lots) cuts them sharply. If you still see runoff, shorten the cycles further.

title: Tree protection zone calculator
text:
Español
Most of a tree’s roots are in the top 12–18 inches of soil and spread well beyond the branches. Driving, stockpiling, trenching or changing the grade over them can kill a mature tree, often a few years later. Before any work, fence off a protection zone.
Measure the trunk at 4½ ft (1.4 m) above the ground. Wrap a tape around it for the circumference, or measure the diameter directly.

title: Tree protection zone calculator
text:
Why trees die after construction
Roots need air as much as water. Compaction from vehicles crushes the pore spaces; fill soil buries roots too deep; trenching cuts them. The tree may look fine for a season or two, using stored energy, then decline from the top down. By the time you see dieback, the damage was done years before.
The zone here scales with the trunk, the tree’s age and how well the species copes, following a widely used arborist approach. The simpler rule of thumb, one foot of radius per inch of trunk diameter, is shown in the working for comparison.

text:
The short version

Trees: never amend the planting hole. Wide hole, native soil, mulch.
Native and low-water plants: usually nothing. Rich soil works against them.
Vegetables: yes, compost every year.
Lawns: improve the soil before seeding. On an existing lawn, aerate and top-dress lightly.
Clay: compost helps; a little sand makes it worse.
Standing water: a drainage problem, not a soil-quality one.

title: Lawn vs low-water landscape: water use calculator
text:
How this is worked out
Plants lose water through their leaves at a rate set mainly by weather: sun, heat, wind and dry air. Weather networks express that as reference evapotranspiration (ETo): what a well-watered grass would use. Each planting uses a share of it: bluegrass close to 80%, buffalograss under half, established low-water shrubs a third or less. Subtract the rain the plants can use, allow for watering that’s never perfectly efficient, and you have the irrigation.
The factors used here are typical values for planning. They’re useful for comparing options, not for setting a controller: for that, use the catch-cup test.

More than places on a map
The places where we work are more than locations where research happens. They are landscapes we have learned from, communities we have worked alongside and relationships that continue long after individual projects end.
Each place has shaped how we approach science in a different way. Some have taught us to look at familiar problems differently; others have shown us the value of local knowledge, shared experience and working with what is available rather than assuming that better science always requires more technology.



Pondering over Hout Bay as we hike from the south side of Table Mountain


We created these pages to share some of those experiences. They are not intended to be complete histories of our research or lists of projects and achievements. Instead, they offer glimpses of the people, places and ideas that have influenced how we work today and what makes our approach different.

title: Where We Work
text:
Different places, shared ideas
Our work spans different landscapes, scientific traditions and ways of understanding the world. What connects them is the belief that useful knowledge grows through exchange: between disciplines, between people with different expertise and between scientific understanding and the places where it matters.



Deep roots searching in the heavily degraded soil (left). Solution, sustainable grazing to increase the water infiltration and organic matter of the heavily eroded and compact soil (right)


The individual stories reflect this diversity. Each has its own history, lessons and connections, but together they form a broader picture of how our work has developed and where it may lead next.

The work continues
A project may end, a research appointment may change or we may move on to another landscape. The knowledge and relationships built along the way do not simply disappear.
RafikiArdhi carries that spirit forward: making knowledge accessible, sharing useful tools and creating opportunities for the next generation.

title: Foundation grading check
text:
Español
Water pooling against a foundation is one of the most expensive problems a house can have. The common building-code guideline is that ground should fall at least 6 inches over the first 10 feet from the house (about 5%). You can check it in an afternoon.
How to measure: drive a stake against the foundation and another 10 ft (3 m) out. Tie a string between them and level it with a line level. At each stake, measure from the string down to the ground. The drop is the outer measurement minus the inner one. Repeat every 10–15 ft along each wall.

title: Foundation grading check
section: Other signs of a grading problem
text:
Other signs of a grading problem

Water standing next to the foundation after rain or irrigation.
Mulch or soil piled up against the siding, often built up over years.
Downspouts that empty right at the wall.
Patios, walks or window wells that have settled so they tip toward the house.
Damp patches, efflorescence (white crust) or musty smells in a basement or crawlspace.

Most of these are cheap to fix compared with foundation repairs.

title: Europe - Learning to See the Landscape
text:
Beyond familiar ground
Europe was where RafikiArdhi’s research story first extended beyond Africa, beyond soil and plants. Through our first research experiences on another continent and our early independent research, we encountered new landscapes, new scientific traditions and different ways of approaching environmental questions such as the restoration of drained peat lands.
Working in unfamiliar places brought an important lesson: good science does not necessarily require the most advanced technology or the largest collection of data. It requires knowing what you are looking at and the curiosity to solve it.



Leaves lower down on the tree turn yellow first as the tree allocates its nitrogen to the roots from the older leaves first

title: Europe - Learning to See the Landscape
text:
Understanding the landscape
Technology can help us measure, model and visualise the environment, but it cannot replace an understanding of how a landscape works. Knowing the area — its soils, geology, history and the processes that shape it — can be more valuable than having access to ever more sophisticated tools.



The NDVI area under the curve for the 2017 growing season of the Czech Republic at a 10 m resolution. Performed through the integral at each pixel on a standard intel CPU laptop


This perspective continues to shape how RafikiArdhi approaches environmental research. Models should help us understand the landscape, not simply produce predictions about it. Methods are most useful when they are grounded in the places they are intended to represent.
In doing so, we have developed a suite of research tools and research checks that do not use any AI or machine learning. They are advanced methods developed not only for free use, but to demonstrate that access to knowledge and where that knowledge comes from is the most important tool RafikiArdhi has.



NDVI trend analysis for different land uses in South Bohemia, Czech Republic

title: Europe - Learning to See the Landscape
text:
Lessons that travel
The experience of working across continents reinforced the value of combining quantitative methods with knowledge of place. Techniques can travel between regions, but their application must account for the conditions, processes and histories that make each landscape distinctive.
For RafikiArdhi, this remains central to our approach: use technology where it adds value, keep the science transparent and never lose sight of the landscape behind the data.



Storm that uplifted trees České Budějovice due to compacted subsoil preventing roots to establish sufficiently (left & right). Dog named “Rafiki” doing his buisness on said trees


Working with the Biology Centre of the Czech Academy of Sciences in České Budějovice, we modelled ecosystem services across the whole of the Czech Republic. With the Department of Horticulture at the University of Bonn, we worked on decision analysis for agroforestry systems across the wider European Union.
Both projects ran into COVID-19. Travel stopped, fieldwork was put on hold and the plans we started with no longer worked. What remained was a laptop, open satellite data and what we knew about the landscapes.



Farm expanding its agroforestry endevours in Western Germany


It was enough. The national vegetation analysis below ran on an ordinary laptop. Decision analysis is built for exactly this situation: it works with what is known, states the uncertainty about the rest, and still gives an answer people can act on. Neither project needed more technology. Both needed a clear understanding of the systems being studied.

title: Landscape quote checker
section: Why quotes are hard to compare
text:
Why quotes are hard to compare

Yards vs tons. A cubic yard of mulch weighs a few hundred pounds; a cubic yard of gravel weighs well over a ton. A price per ton and a price per yard can’t be compared unless you know what the material weighs. The checker converts using typical weights; ask the supplier for theirs.
Delivery. A delivery fee spread over a small load makes the price per unit look high. Compare quotes for the same quantity.
Extra for settling. Loose material settles after spreading, so a fair quote includes a little more than the measured volume, usually 5–25% depending on the material. A quote for double what you need is not “a little extra”.
Bags. Bag sizes vary (1, 1.5, 2 or 3 cubic feet). Check the bag size before comparing bag prices.

Use the materials calculator to work out exactly how much you need for an odd-shaped area.

title: Rain barrel and rainwater harvesting calculator
text:
Making the most of it

Barrels fill fast and empty slowly. Use the water between storms so there’s room for the next one.
A soaker hose or drip line works on barrel pressure if the barrel is raised on blocks; sprinklers don’t.
For larger volumes, directing downspouts into planted areas or a rain garden stores water in the soil itself, often more of it than barrels hold, and is allowed almost everywhere.

    Reading the results
    
      Nugget : sill is the share of variation you can't predict at your sampling scale: measurement error plus variation over distances shorter than your closest samples. Under 0.25 is strong spatial dependence, 0.25–0.75 moderate, over 0.75 weak.
      Range is the distance beyond which samples stop telling you about each other. If your samples are mostly further apart than the range, kriging can do little better than the mean, however good the software.
      RMSE vs. the mean is the real test: it shows how much spatial prediction actually adds. A map made by kriging is only worth its colours if this is clearly above zero.
      MSDR and interval coverage show whether the uncertainty is honest. MSDR near 1 and coverage near 90% mean the kriging variance can be trusted; otherwise the uncertainty map is too optimistic or too cautious.
      Two limits that are rarely stated. Cross-validated RMSE can't fall much below the square root of the nugget, because that part of the variation isn't predictable from neighbours. And when samples are further apart than the range, RMSE approaches the standard deviation of the data. A published RMSE well below these limits usually means the validation points weren't independent of the calibration data, the variogram came from a different dataset, or the error was reported on a different scale.

What we believe

 Build on what exists. Old surveys and past projects are worth more than people think. We update knowledge instead of replace it.
 Honest uncertainty. Every answer comes with how far it can be trusted. We propogate uncertainties and make them informative.
 No AI, no black boxes. Our methods follow the processes behind the environment, so every result can be traced and checked.
 Science in your own language. Our tools and keys come in the languages people actually speak, not only English. Want to help?
 Land is shared. Healthy land includes the animals that live with us and the attitude we bring to it.



Homeowners: open science
Practical home and landscape decisions informed by the same scientific principles researchers use, from applying Darcy’s and Jurin’s laws for irrigation design to using calculus to estimate sod quantities for irregular lawns.
